item.title: Jetten cabinet survives crisis talks for now, deadlock continues
item.description:
Jetten cabinet survives crisis talks for now, deadlock continues

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch cabinet’s crisis talks ended in deadlock on Friday after more than seven hours, and the coalition will survive for the time being, though talks will continue over the weekend.

Prime minister Rob Jetten met  right-wing liberal VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz and Christian Democrat CDA deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink on Friday morning, following Thursday night’s vote on the tax plan, which the VVD says broke the coalition agreement.

Yesilgöz, speaking at a press conference after the talks, said the political situation cannot continue as things stand. She described the current minority coalition as a “failed experiment” and said that a government collapse was a “possible solution”, while acknowledging no one wants to plunge the country into another election.

Jetten, who spoke before her, said that “things have not gone well recently, and that is affecting mutual relations”. “That can and must be better: substantively, politically, and personally.”

While the cabinet has not yet collapsed, VVD sources told the Telegraaf that no progress had been made and the impasse continues.

If the talks had ended on Friday, “it could have gone wrong”, Jetten said.

item.title: Health insurance premiums will rise next year
item.description:
Health insurance premiums will rise next year

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Health insurance companies are set to increase premiums in 2027, pushing up the cost of a basic package up by as much as €17 a month.

Companies were required to announce the cost of their premiums by midnight on Thursday and the cost will rise sharply across the board next year.

Insurer DSW, traditionally the first to publish its rates, announced in October that the price for its premium will go up by €14.75 a month.

The most popular basic insurance at Zilveren Kruis is rising by €5.70 euros to €164.95 euros, while at CZ the basic insurance will soon cost €177.25, an increase of more than €17 compared to last year.

Last year, premiums were able to remain virtually unchanged due to more money in the health insurance fund.

Health insurance companies attribute the rise to the aging population, which has more health care needs, as well as the increase in wages for healthcare employees and gas prices.

item.title: Two arrested for Prinsjesdag train sabotage
item.description:
Two arrested for Prinsjesdag train sabotage

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police have arrested two people in connection with the sabotage on the railway during Prinsjesdag, the public prosecution service (OM) announced on Friday.

A 49-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman from Drenthe were arrested on Thursday. According to the OM, the pair remain suspects but there was not enough evidence to keep them in custody.

Train services across the country were disrupted in September in what network operators described an act of coordinated sabotage. The attacks took place during Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in The Hague and one of the biggest days in the Dutch political calendar.

Steel pipes were attached to the tracks at multiple locations across the country, disrupting rail service nationwide.

It is not yet known who was behind the attacks. On the same day, tractor tires, hay bales, and pallets were lit on fire at various locations. Some of those incidents were tied to farmer activists.

The Farmers Defence Force, responsible for recent motorway disruptions, said it was not responsible but that “wild actions” by individual farmers had been expected on budget day.

The two suspects are the first to be arrested in the case.

item.title: The Hague is the tile “whipping” champion
item.description:
The Hague is the tile “whipping” champion

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

No city has done more to whip their gardens into shape than The Hague, which took home the Golden Tile prize for removing the most paving stones from its gardens, totalling a record 507,000 citywide, breaking the previous record by nearly 50,000.

The NK Tegelwippen, or Dutch National Tile Removal Championship, pits councils against one another to see who can free up the most green space.

According to the organisation, this makes neighbourhoods more attractive, combats flood and rising temperatures and gives children more areas for play.

“It is fantastic that we are still breaking records. It shows that perseverance pays off and that residents consider greenery in the city increasingly important,” Joris Wijsmuller, the director of Duurzaam Den Haag, said in a statement.

Some 150,000 tiles were taken out by residents, schools, sports clubs, and companies participated in the event, according to the council. The remainder were removed by the city in public spaces.

The Hague also won the title in 2021 and 2022.

item.title: Three’s a crowd: Will Jetten’s tax bill kill the cabinet?
item.description:
Three’s a crowd: Will Jetten’s tax bill kill the cabinet?

November 13, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

There is an old medical joke about a surgeon who declares: “The operation was a complete success, but the patient died.”

After months of chaotic, gruelling negotiations, Rob Jetten achieved a majority in parliament for his tax bill on Thursday night, but his coalition is in tatters. The right-wing liberal VVD were so incensed by the deal the other two partners, Jetten’s D66 and the Christian Democrats (CDA), struck with the left-wing Pro that they voted against the entire plan, which had been extensively drafted and redrafted by the VVD finance minister, Eelco Heinen.

The party’s leader, Dilan Yesilgöz, denounced it as “a bad deal for the Netherlands” and demanded a “fundamental reset” of the centre-right coalition. Essentially, she wanted the prime minister to switch his cabinet off and switch it on again.

The millionaires’ tax knife twist 
Strikingly, the amendment that D66, CDA and Pro agreed on Wednesday afternoon was a milder version of one that the VVD had seemed willing to tolerate earlier in the week. Pro wanted to raise an extra €1.5 billion in wealth taxes in order to pay for an income tax cut for the lowest earners. D66 and CDA had negotiated the amount down to €1 billion and built in counterbalancing measures to protect people with modest savings – at an earlier stage one of the key concerns for the VVD. Its impact, even on the private investors it was aimed at, was marginal.

But none of that mattered. For the VVD, the deal was unacceptable because it crossed a red line – raising taxes on successful, hard-working entrepreneurs – and it was drawn up behind their backs between their coalition partners and Pro.

Jesse Klaver, the leader of Pro, then twisted the knife by describing the measure as a “millionaires’ tax”, a phrase that went down like cold gravel in the throats of not just the VVD, but CDA leader Henri Bontenbal.

The seeds of the crisis were sown around 10 days earlier, as a reconstruction in AD.nl has found, when the coalition parties agreed to enter what commentators immediately called an “open marriage”. After months of abortive attempts to strike a collective deal with a divided opposition that balanced the interests of left and right, the three parties would try to form separate majorities for their own priorities. It would allow D66 and CDA to pair up with Pro and Volt while the VVD could court the right-wing opposition block of JA21, the farmers’ party BBB and the orthodox Protestant SGP. As a last resort, they could even vote on opposite sides when the amendments were tabled in parliament, if it meant that the tax bill and the coalition survived.

Unagreed terms 
The problem was, none of the parties had agreed on the terms of the open marriage. And what the VVD hadn’t reckoned with was that D66 and CDA would go all the way with Pro and produce an amendment that seemed calculated to hurt them. D66 and CDA protested that they had kept their partners informed throughout the negotiations and even invited them to the table. But the VVD’s whole reason for joining the coalition in the first place was to keep the left-wing Pro out of power, as D66 and CDA knew all too well.

For Yesilgöz, the amendment represented the very outcome that she had entered the partnership to avoid, and Klaver’s press conference and Instagram reel to celebrate the millionaires’ tax were simply rubbing salt into the wound. To extend the analogy, it was like agreeing to an arranged marriage only to see your partner immediately phone up the ex-girlfriend he told you was no threat and take her for dinner at the Ritz.

None of this should obscure the extent to which the VVD engineered their own downfall. The minority cabinet was built on unstable foundations because the VVD wanted to shut out the opposition party that would have the strongest hand in the upcoming negotiations. When the coalition agreement was published, they took out billboards to parade their achievements, such as retaining mortgage interest tax relief.

The final betrayal
From the outset the VVD have focused more on defending their red lines within the coalition than finding the opposition votes they need to pass their legislation. It allowed Pro to exploit the deadlock to torpedo key VVD policies such as the €6.5 billion of welfare cuts. The budget amendment was the final betrayal for the VVD, but it was also the inevitable outcome of a process in which the party had refused to build any kind of constructive relationship with Pro, while D66 and CDA had reached out to unlikely partners such as Gidi Markuszower’s far-right DNA. And when the VVD decided to reject its own budget deal, its partners delivered a final humiliation by salvaging it with the support of a pair of fringe parties on the left: Denk and the animal rights party PvdD.

What happens next is unclear. The VVD, stung by what they see as a deep betrayal, want the coalition to renew its vows. Jetten prefers to talk about a “restart”, the language usually used for businesses that have called in the receivers. Yesilgöz almost goaded the other parties to try their luck with Pro in a new combination, but that would leave the cabinet still nine votes short of a majority and a hostile opposition dominated by the right. Jesse Klaver may well have overplayed his hand with his “pick me” posts on social media.

But new elections are an equally risky option for three parties whose standing in the opinion polls has been further damaged by the tax plan saga. And if the coalition survives in its current form, it will be as a marriage of inconvenience. Not for the first time, politics and matrimony have turned out to be a toxic mix.

item.title: Nine men arrested in major Rotterdam drugs investigation

Nine men arrested in major Rotterdam drugs investigation

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nine people have been arrested in Rotterdam as part of a major drug dealing investigation, according to regional broadcaster RTV Rijnmond.

Raids were carried out on Monday and led to the seizure of cars, cash and drugs.

Eight of the men are Rotterdam residents and one is from The Hague; they are being charged with membership of a criminal drugs organisation and three are are also suspected of money laundering.

What types of drugs were involved has not been disclosed. All suspects are between 27 and 40 years old, and police have reportedly not ruled out further arrests.

item.title: Narcis by Judith Fanto takes home top book prize
item.description:
Narcis by Judith Fanto takes home top book prize

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A novel about a Dutchman living in Austria during the interwar period has been awarded the 2026 NS Public Prize.

Narcis by Judith Fanto follows Manno, who moves from Haarlem to Vienna following the death of his mother and finds a circle of friends, bonds that are tested as Hitler rises to power.

Fanto described the honour as “wonderful” during a ceremony on Thursday evening. “This appreciation from the readers is the exuberant culmination of years of work in silence,” she said.

She takes home €7,500 and a sculpture in recognition.

The award, now in its 25th edition, is a collaboration between the Foundation for Collective Promotion of the Dutch Book and Dutch railway operator NS.

More than 131,000 readers cast their votes and Narcis beat five other works, including The Superfluous by Herman Koch.

item.title: Warnings as hackers begin exploiting Microsoft outage
item.description:
Warnings as hackers begin exploiting Microsoft outage

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch pharmacists’ organisation KNMP has issued warnings that phishing emails are circulating as hackers attempt to exploit the ongoing Microsoft outage.

Microsoft software, which includes widely used email and communication tools like Outlook and Teams, has been down in much of the world since Thursday evening.

While the company says it has nothing to do with a cybersecurity breach, hackers are apparently attempting to take advantage of the situation by sending phishing emails that appear as messages from Microsoft offering to restore or update software.

The KNMP is urging people not to trust the emails. They are likely malicious attempts to gain control of customer data. Microsoft never sends such emails anyway, and communicates about its outages through its online channels.

Hundreds of millions of people use Microsoft apps daily for their work, making this potentially the “most severe technology outage in history”, a tech analyst told the BBC.

Dutch users of Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 were still impacted on Friday morning. By around 8.15am, Dutch outage tracker allestoringen.nl had logged almost 2,800 complaints about Outlook, nearly 700 about Microsoft 365 and just over 200 about Teams.

The situation was said to be improving by 1pm, with many people in the Netherlands able to access their emails again.

The University of Twente warned of disruption, and regional broadcasters Omroep Flevoland and RTV Utrecht said they were having trouble receiving email, according to ANP.

Microsoft said that the outage was caused by an “increased load” on infrastructure, with a number of servers unexpectedly offline, but no question of a cyberattack, the company wrote on social media.

With 430 million global users of Microsoft 365 software alone, the BBC analyst said the outage could well cause billions of dollars in losses.

item.title: Turning 65 in 2032? You’ve got about 21 years left, says CBS
item.description:
Turning 65 in 2032? You’ve got about 21 years left, says CBS

November 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

If you hit 65 in 2032, you can expect to live another 21 years or so – a bit less than the statisticians estimated this time last year.

National statistics office CBS now puts life expectancy for 65-year-olds in 2032 at 21.08 years, down from the 21.14 years it forecast in 2025. Life expectancy has slowly been rising since Covid knocked it down.

The numbers matter because the social affairs minister uses it to set the state pension (AOW) age, which is tied to life expectancy by law.

The AOW age is already fixed at 67 until the end of 2027, and at 67 and three months from 2028 to 2031. The 2032 figure will be decided on the basis of this new forecast.

In 1950, 65-year-olds could expect to live another 14.3 years. By 2019 that had risen to 20.1 years, before Covid knocked it back to 19.5 in both 2020 and 2021. Last year it was back up to 20.1 years.

Women still outlive men, with a gap of 1.9 years at age 65 in 2025. Men have now clawed their way back to their pre-pandemic level, but women haven’t quite got there yet.
